comments.body:
🤖 Correction to a recommendation I left in an earlier comment. I suggested a one-rack A/B on `--save-checkpoints` to confirm that the hero's per-step `broadcast_one_to_all` creates a communicator inventory the reproduction lacks. I have now run it, and that test cannot work on one rack. Anyone picking this up should not spend a window on it.

Ran at hero shape with `--save-checkpoints --checkpoint-minutes 600`, which exercises the collective without ever performing the 5.4 TB write, and with the step-sharding fix disabled: 164 steps, 16.9 s/it, no stall.

The reason it is not a real test is in the counter. `Init COMPLETE` appears **64 times, once per rank — a single communicator**. At one rack the `(16, 4)` process mesh *is* the same 64 ranks as the expert-parallel clique, so `broadcast_one_to_all` reuses that communicator and creates no distinct rank group. At eleven racks the mesh is `(176, 4)` and spans all 704 ranks, so its rank groups exist nowhere else in the job. The structural difference I wanted to probe only exists at multi-rack, so a clean single-rack result says nothing about it either way.

That matters beyond this one experiment, because it closes the single-rack search on structural grounds rather than by exhaustion of ideas. Two independent reasons now, both measured:

- Symmetric windows are registered only by the ragged path (`--xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`), so additional communicators and expert-domain splitting add no window pressure and do not emulate eleven racks.
- The last identified per-step difference, the checkpointer's `broadcast_one_to_all`, collapses onto the expert-parallel clique at `(16, 4)`.

Note also that `save_checkpoints=False` means no checkpointer object is constructed at all (`train.py:1031`), so every reproduction attempt in this issue executed that collective exactly zero times. That remains the only per-step structural difference between the configuration that hung twice and the ones that did not — it simply cannot be tested below eleven racks.

Nothing here changes the standing conclusion: the locus is established (the kernel's copy loops are bounded, so the barrier is the only place this can hang) and the unreportability is explained, but the trigger is undetermined and needs the failure state observed. The capture path is armed by default on the ragged transport, so a recurrence should name itself.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Retitled from "hangs on one rack at d6144 hero scale after a watch step" to drop the watch-step attribution, which the evidence no longer supports.

The original framing was that two executables — a plain train step and a `diagnostic_watch_step` — alias the symmetric-memory arena, and that the hang lands on the first plain step after a watch step. The deployed commit sets `WatchMode.INLINE` (`launch_scaling_ladder.py:216`), so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built: `jit_train_step` computes the watch statistics on every step and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. The hanging step was byte-identical to the step before it.

The timing correlation is also weaker than the title implied. With `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, attempt 1 completed step 54000, a watch-boundary step, and hung on 54001 — immediately after. But attempt 0 completed **54071** and hung entering 54072, two steps past the 54070 boundary. One attempt fits the pattern and one does not, so "after a watch step" is not a property of the failure.

Worth keeping from the original framing: there really are two executables per rank sharing one arena, and that part is confirmed at hero scale (1408 arena-window registrations across 704 ranks, exactly two per rank). The cause is not the watch step but the step counter's inferred sharding, which is #8861's root cause and is fixed on `mcwitt/8870-repro`. Whether that aliasing is also what makes this issue's hang possible is still open.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Result of the 2026-09-04 eleven-rack telemetry window. No hang in 183 job-steps, but the new barrier instrumentation produced the first *measured* asymmetry between racks this issue has had, and it is not hardware.

**What ran.** `mcwitt/8870-repro` @ `0ee0880b77`, which is the hung commit `8e48cdb3ca` plus diagnostics and nothing else (not rebased; the six main-line commits past `8e48cdb3ca` touch no training code). PJRT wheel `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-3091aa7302d8`: device kernels built against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7, both LSA barrier waits bounded at ~45 s with a record naming rank, slot and phase on expiry, and — new for this run — a per-thunk, per-phase high-water mark of the barrier wait, logged at INFO whenever it doubles above 1 ms. Hero-identical otherwise: the #8861 fix switched off so both aliasing windows are present (confirmed two per rank), the checkpointer constructed with a 600-minute interval so its per-step `broadcast_one_to_all` runs, `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NVLS`, core dump armed. Restored `step-54000`, 11 racks / 704 GPUs / batch 11264, system priority. Steps 54000–54183 at 17–19 s/it and 23% MFU, loss 1.2364 at 54000 exactly as in both hero attempts. Zero barrier timeouts, zero bounds violations, zero errors. The JAX compilation cache hit with the new wheel, since the cache key does not include the PJRT build (`cache_key.py` hashes `jaxlib`'s version and `platform_version`, which is the CUDA runtime), so startup was six minutes.

**The measurement.** Post-copy waits never exceed 4.2 ms on any rank. Pre-copy waits on racks 0–7 (tasks 0–127) never exceed 10.5 ms, with per-rack medians of 5.6–9.9 ms. Pre-copy waits on racks 8, 9 and 10 (tasks 128–175) reach **158, 103 and 128 ms**, with per-rack medians of 157, 98 and 124 ms — i.e. essentially every rank on those three racks saw it. Full sweep of all 704 ranks is in `scratch/8870/window/w3-waitmarks.csv`.

**Event structure.** Collapsing the ≥50 ms lines by timestamp gives six events during the run (a seventh at 23:31:46 coincides with the cancel at 23:31:50 and is teardown). Each is a single launch on a single rack in which **63 of the 64 ranks wait the same ~N ms** — so one rank arrived late to the pre-copy barrier and its 63 clique peers waited for it. The rank that did not wait is the straggler, and it is a different rank on a different node every time:

| time (UTC) | rack | waiters | median wait | rank that did not wait | node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 22:36:36 | 9 | 63 | 98 ms | task 145 rank 3 | `s4gwxs64` |
| 22:36:56 | 8 | 63 | 101 ms | task 136 rank 2 | `s8mtxs64` |
| 22:37:29 | 10 | 63 | 81 ms | task 168 rank 2 | `s9jyxs64` |
| 22:38:33 | 8 | 45 | 52 ms | (19 below threshold) | — |
| 22:40:30 | 10 | 63 | 124 ms | task 162 rank 3 | `s2grxs64` |
| 22:45:18 | 8 | 63 | 158 ms | task 134 rank 3 | `s7qvxs64` |

Roughly steps 2, 2, 3, 8, 13 and 28. Six different nodes, six different ranks, three racks, never racks 0–7. A bad GPU or host would recur on itself; this roams. And these are sticky maxima that only log on a doubling, so a repeat at the same magnitude is invisible — the true event count is at least this and probably higher.

**Placement.** The task-to-node map was identical to the hero's own 176-task placement and to last night's second window; the first window differed at rack indices 0 and 1, so the index is "whichever racks are free" and is not a stable identifier. What is stable: rack 8 here is **the same sixteen nodes, 16 of 16, as the slice that stalled in hero attempt 0** (tasks 128–143, `s38vxs64 … shmsxs64`), and racks 9 and 10 were the same physical nodes in every one of these placements too. So this data cannot separate "the last three replica indices" from "these three specific racks". Against the hardware reading: attempt 1's stuck slice (tasks 64–79, rack 4) shows nothing here, 7.6 ms maximum, indistinguishable from the healthy racks.

**Reading it, carefully.** Pre-copy is the rendezvous before any peer store, so a long pre-copy wait means EP-clique peers had not yet *reached* the ragged kernel; the copies themselves are not slow (post-copy is flat). One rank per event arriving 80–160 ms late, recurring, only on replica indices 8–10 of the 11-wide `replica_dcn` axis, points at something rank-order-dependent upstream of the all-to-all: the two `nranks 11` replica-axis communicators that rank 0 reports (ring or tree position of the last three replicas), the data loader's per-replica shard timing, the checkpointer's `(176, 4)` broadcast that was live for the first time in a reproduction, or host-side work that lands on those ranks. None of that is tested. What it is not: a hang — 160 ms is three orders of magnitude short of 45 s, and in 183 steps nothing grew toward one. Whether the hang is the extreme tail of this distribution or a different phenomenon is exactly the open question, but until now there was no distribution to speak of.

**Also recorded from this run.** Communicator inventory on rank 0 with the checkpointer live: `nranks 64`, `704`, and two `nranks 11`. Two arena windows per rank (1408 across 704 ranks), as in the hang. `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG` was dropped after measuring that it alone produced 98.5% of task-log volume (one `IPC reuse buffer` line per collective per peer, 356 MB per task per hour, ~63 GB per window into finelog); without it a task logs ~5 MB. The hero resumed from the forced `step-61806` at 23:35Z and is running.

**Next.** (1) Make recurrence measurable: a per-launch histogram, or reset the marks every N launches, so the event rate and its trend over a longer run are observable rather than inferred from doublings. (2) Separate position from hardware: a placement that lands different physical racks at replica indices 8–10 — the Kueue gate that blocked today's smoke (#8925) makes this awkward but it is the decisive test. (3) Catch the straggler in the act: a host-side timestamp around the ragged thunk on every rank would say what the late rank was doing — the barrier marks say only that it was late. (4) Repeat with the #8861 fix on, to see whether one executable per rank changes the tail.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The hung run pinned a QuACK version with a concrete matrix-multiplication (GEMM) scheduler defect. This is a new lead; the cause of #8870 remains unproved.

The deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca` [pins QuACK 0.6.1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L96), and the archived attempt-0 task-1 setup log confirms `quack-kernels==0.6.1`. The ragged backend's [activation GEMMs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/sonic_cute.py#L57) use Cluster Launch Control (CLC), which lets resident GPU thread blocks take over work from pending clusters, with variable-length expert groups. The audited package source matches the [0.6.1 release](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/02c7f69881737731173a6a009aeb6f032e449b61/quack/tile_scheduler.py#L504).

That scheduler can observe a failed CLC cancellation, leave its work loop, and then issue more cancellations through its unconditional `cancel_pending_tail` path. NVIDIA's [PTX specification](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.0.0/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#parallel-synchronization-and-communication-instructions-clusterlaunchcontrol-try-cancel) defines further cancellation requests after a GPU thread block observes failure as undefined behavior. The drain also issues asynchronous requests without waiting for their responses before exit.

Upstream [58cb592a1a6e](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6e) replaces this path with a conditional, response-checked drain and a separate response buffer. Its [investigation](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/58cb592a1a6e/AI/clc_spurious_invalid_investigation.md) reports stale GEMM output tiles with a second process sharing the GPU and multiple queued GEMM launches, plus a separate GPU-error hazard from requests still in flight at block exit. Those experiments used B300; they do not establish the behavior of our GB200 run. The specification violation does not prove it caused our silent hang, and the cached GPU binary from the original run has not yet been checked against that source.

If this defect prevents a rank's GEMM from completing, the other ranks in its expert-parallel group could wait indefinitely at the next ragged barrier. The [earlier bounded-copy-loop argument](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5537281960) does not exclude a preceding kernel that never completes. Next is a comparison of the original scheduler and a narrow drain fix under finite competing GPU work, checking for incorrect outputs, timeouts and GPU errors at the production matrix dimensions. Each version will use a separate compilation cache so the treatment executes newly compiled code.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The [QuACK scheduler lead](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5548674783) now has a GB200 output-corruption reproduction. In a four-GPU comparison, the original scheduler left output regions unwritten in three cases with a competing process. The narrow drain fix and the no-Cluster-Launch-Control (no-CLC) control had no detected errors.

| Arm | Quiet cases passed | Contention cases passed | Measured launches |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Original QuACK 0.6.1 | 3/3 | 1/4 | 12,080 |
| Narrow upstream drain fix | 3/3 | 4/4 | 21,000 |
| No CLC | 3/3 | 3/3 | 18,000 |

Each case used a fresh process and isolated compilation cache, BF16 constant inputs, 16 queued GEMMs with distinct outputs, and synchronization before reset and validation. The contender ran matrix multiplications in a separate process on the same GPU. Original and fixed arms each repeated one contention case on a different GPU, accounting for their fourth case. The failures occurred on three different GPUs; all incorrect elements retained the output's sentinel value. An independent harness audit found no reset, aliasing, layout or numerical-reference error explaining the retained sentinel values. The three tested shapes were synthetic; this initial comparison did not use the original run's recovered three-expert dimensions. Passing cases reached 3,000 launches after 3.59–16.92 seconds of measured work. Failed cases stopped at their first bad batch, so aggregate counts do not estimate a long-run failure rate.

The historical binary audit also found the unsafe drain in four of the nine CuTe cache keys logged by the original attempt-0 task-1, representing three distinct binaries. Original cache objects predate the run and match the audited bytes in the historical snapshot spanning its lookups. This establishes historical cache contents, rather than an independent dump of the hung process's GPU memory.

The connection to the silent training hang remains unproved: these failures returned incorrect outputs without timing out. A repeat is running with dimensions recovered from the original saved config and source, using synthetic balanced routing. A same-process competing-stream test will address the difference between this reproduction and the training workload. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/340) preserves the evidence boundary and experiment constraints.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The production hero — on the **pooled-wave** transport, not ragged — stalled silently for fifteen minutes today and then died of an NVLink fault, and it originated on one of the three racks the telemetry window flagged. This is the strongest evidence so far that #8870's root cause is a fabric fault on specific NVL72 domains rather than anything in the ragged kernel, which merely fails silently where NCCL's host path eventually fails loudly.

**Timeline (2026-09-05, UTC), `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` on the same 176 nodes and the same rack map as both 09-02 hang attempts and the 09-04 window.** Last step 65069 completed at 17:19:31. Nothing was logged by any rank for the next fifteen minutes; Iris's py-spy dumps at 17:21 and 17:31 show every sampled rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), i.e. blocked on the device — the #8870 shape exactly. At **17:34:36.549 task 162 rank 1 on `s2grxs64` (rack 10, NVLink domain `dh1-r137`)** logged the first `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over nvlink or a hardware error` (from `cudaFreeAsync`, `gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:414`); the other rack-10 nodes followed within 0.5 s, racks 2 and 6 by 17:34:37.8, and every rack by 17:34:43 — 88 of 176 tasks logged the fault, the rest were taken down by fate sharing. Iris restarted the gang; it resumed from the hourly temp `step-64944` at 17:38, so the event cost 125 steps plus 20 minutes. It is healthy again (step 65623 at 20 s/step).

**Why this bears on the ragged hangs.** The pooled-wave transport moves data through NCCL's host-driven path, where a fabric fault eventually surfaces as a contained CUDA error and the driver tears the context down. The ragged device kernel spins in an LSA barrier with `abortFlag == nullptr` and, on the wheel that hung, no bounded wait, so the same fault produces fifteen minutes of silence followed by the 900 s progress watchdog — which is what both 09-02 attempts looked like. The fifteen-minute latency before the contained error is itself notable: the fault was in progress, invisible, for as long as the ragged hangs lasted before the watchdog fired.

**The three racks now line up with three independent fabric observations.** Rack 10 (`dh1-r137`): today's fault origin; and `s2grxs64` is the node that supplied the 22:40:30 straggler in the window (task 162, 124 ms). Rack 8 (`dh1-r129`): the 09-02 attempt-0 stall node set; a 5.009 s NVLS multicast bind at window startup (9-12× every other rack); the only repeat straggler node; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 is a flapping NVLink — 505 recovery events lifetime, +3 in a 21-minute sample last night and +1 more since, read-only from the running hero, the only counter that moved anywhere in a five-rack sweep. Rack 9 (`dh1-r136`): stragglers in the window, no counter evidence yet. Racks 0-7 show none of this. Rack 10's own GPU-side link counters did not move across today's fault, so the error is on the switch side or a non-link hardware error; node `dmesg`/XIDs are not visible from inside the containers.

**What this changes.** The 09-04 deep-dive (`scratch/8870/window/deepdive/`, eleven streams) had already falsified the cross-rack collective-stall mechanism and left "a per-GPU transient of 25-160 ms, ≥11× more frequent on racks 8-10, with nothing upstream of the GPU to blame." A fabric fault that stalls whatever is crossing a link, escalating occasionally to a contained error or a permanent stall, fits every measurement in this issue, including why attempt 0 hung on rack 8 and why one-rack reproductions on healthy racks never reproduced anything. It does not explain attempt 1 (rack 4, `dh1-r124`), which shows nothing in any sweep; that may be a fourth domain or a different event.

**Untested but now less likely as the cause:** the NCCL 2.29.7/2.30.7 compile skew (the ragged wheel that hung compiled its kernels against 2.29.7; every diagnostic wheel since used 2.30.7). It remains the one code difference between the hung configuration and every clean run, and an A/B wheel exists (`marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-355d8f15cc25`), but today's fault happened with no ragged kernel in the picture at all.

**Asks.** (1) Infra: node-level `dmesg`/XID history and fabric-manager/NVSwitch logs for `dh1-r137` around 17:19-17:35 today and `dh1-r129` around 2026-09-04 22:35:04-09; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 as a flapping link. (2) Before the next ragged deployment, a pre-flight that reads NVLink error counters and times the first symmetric-window bind per rack, and refuses racks that stand out. (3) The next 11-rack window should run the per-node 1 Hz GPU/NVLink sampler now on the branch (`MARIN_DEBUG_GPU_SAMPLER_SECONDS=1`) with the per-launch barrier reports, so a link recovery and a barrier stall can be joined at one-second resolution.

Data: `scratch/8870/window/hero-20260905-fault-ranks.txt` (first fault per task/rank/node), `gpuhealth{,2,3}/` (three read-only counter sweeps).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 The [QuACK upgrade branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/upgrade-quack-064) includes the [upstream CLC scheduling fix](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6ef85a69e37d0b4eb50217b59d20ca). [The follow-up commit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/66c5e81628) adapts the JAX tensor views to QuACK 0.6.4's batch-first calling convention. The original training hang remains unexplained.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The September 9 production stall adds evidence for a timing-sensitive synchronization failure after a slow data fetch. This is a hypothesis; the blocked GPU operation and root cause remain unknown.

The affected attempt was `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step81k-coord-1515615f`, with 176 tasks and 704 GPU processes. Its setup logs on tasks 94 and 149 report `quack-kernels==0.6.4`, so this recurrence does not support treating the QuACK upgrade as sufficient to prevent hangs. All times below are UTC on September 9.

- Step 81,758 completed at 19:59:39.838 with loss 1.2321685553. No later completed step was retained for this execution.
- At 19:59:50, all 704 processes reported a data fetch taking at least 10 seconds. Subsequently 680 reported at least 20 seconds, 271 at least 30 seconds, and 19 at least 40 seconds. The final warning was at 20:00:20.119. These counts use distinct task/local-rank pairs.
- Retained Python stack captures at 20:09:40–20:09:54 cover all 704 training processes: every main thread was in `train_step` at `moe_hero_ep/train.py:1176`, and every data-prefetch thread was waiting to enqueue into a full queue. This argues against an ongoing data-loader wait as the condition sustaining the stall. Python stacks do not identify the executing GPU kernel.
- NCCL RAS snapshots at 20:07:56 and 20:17:56 show unchanged AllReduce count ranges of 6,238–6,241 across 64 communicators, plus a range of 10,822–10,824 on one communicator. Both snapshots reported all ranks present, with no missing, unresponsive, or considered-dead ranks across 76 communicators; no communicator records were omitted or invalid. Persistent count divergence does not establish that NCCL caused the stall: an earlier GPU operation can prevent a rank from reaching the next collective.

A candidate trigger is unequal rank arrival after the slow fetch exposing a synchronization defect in the ragged collective or another GPU operation. The warnings describe background prefetch, and per-rank fetch-completion and train-step-entry timestamps are missing, so they do not establish that the delayed fetch fed the stalled step. The earlier [NVLink fault evidence](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) remains relevant; this observation does not exclude hardware or fabric faults.

The discriminating test is a controlled replay with selected ranks delayed before a training step, comparing ragged A2A with the alternative pooled-wave expert-communication backend and capturing per-rank entry times plus verbose RAS and GPU/native stacks if it stalls. That test has not run.

The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) preserves the attempt/execution identifiers and Finelog query scope for the retained evidence.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Audit of the eleven-rack evidence as of September 9, 22:21 UTC: the NCCL 2.30.7 header build is a promising mitigation, but the record does not support treating all four clean windows as tests of that change. My subjective confidence that the header update materially reduces or resolves the specific ragged-A2A hang is about 60%; this is an engineering judgment, not a statistical posterior or a claim that the failure is eliminated.

Installation logs and distinct process-zero `train_loss` steps give this corrected inventory. Counts include the completed step carrying the restored step number; the earlier comments reported slightly smaller counts at their observation cutoffs.

| Eleven-rack run | PJRT build | Compiled NCCL headers | Completed step records | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| September 3, `ra2a-8870-w1-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 165: 54000–54164 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w2-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 72: 54000–54071 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w3-hero11` | `3091aa7302d8` | 2.30.7 | 185: 54000–54184 | No recorded hang; instrumented wheel |
| September 9, production attempt `72aad6e7` | `b183c591142c` | 2.30.7 | 217: 81716–81932 | Still progressing at the cutoff |

All four used NCCL runtime 2.30.7. The verified newer-header exposure is therefore 402 completed steps across two runs; 237 additional clean steps used the old headers. The earlier statement that every clean reproduction used newer headers was incorrect. The [first two windows](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5534213125) also omitted the checkpointer's per-step broadcast. The [third window](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5547757908) restored that broadcast but added bounded barriers, wait instrumentation, initialization waits and post-collective device-to-host copies. Its success cannot isolate the header change.

Today's run is stronger evidence. It has 176 running tasks, 704 GPU processes, PJRT `b183c591142c`, NCCL runtime 2.30.7 and QuACK 0.6.4. The wheel's source change from production's `3a8f3392723e` is the two-line NCCL build-default update in [XLA PR #22](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/pull/22). The live `train.py` hash matches main, and the batch-ready host barrier is absent. The preceding production attempt `1515615f` used PJRT `3a8f3392723e` with NCCL 2.29.7 headers and runtime 2.30.7; it completed 43 steps from the same restored step 81716 before stalling. Today’s wheel omits the September 4 diagnostic barrier timeouts and device-to-host wait-record copies. This is useful evidence against those diagnostic copies or the proposed host barrier being necessary for the current improvement. It is still one uninstrumented success, with build toolchain, allocation and timing differences, rather than a randomized wheel A/B or a tested restart sequence. Old-header clean windows and the [September 5 pooled-wave run’s contained NVLink error](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) keep alternatives credible; that separate failure shows hardware can also cause a similar stall.

There is also preliminary numerical and performance evidence. Comparing today’s run with `1515615f` over matched steps 81726–81758, loss differed by at most 0.000110 nats, with mean treatment-minus-control +0.0000076. The mean of the reported `throughput_mean_mfu` samples was 21.626% for the new wheel versus 22.110% for the earlier attempt, a decrease of 0.484 percentage points (2.19% relative). These 33 matched steps are observational and do not establish a performance regression or non-regression. Sustained training and restart validation remain open.

For reproducibility, the historical execution IDs are `iris:227df97f1c61d78c`, `iris:8a8e59dcdce56776` and `iris:153389937ce684a7`; today's control and treatment are `iris:a8d3026cb58a0341` and `iris:aa61bafbfdef1160`. Counts use `levanter.metrics`, `name='train_loss'`, `process_index=0`, deduplicated by execution and step. The Marin hub lagged today's regional metrics: 196 records through 22:13:27 UTC on the hub, with the remaining 21 through 22:21:17 UTC verified on `cw-us-east-08a`. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) and [wheel-pin PR #9062](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9062) track the current mitigation.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The source audit found two concrete deadlocks in the remote GIN branch, but neither explains the measured `gin=false` hero path. Zero-size updates skip completion signals that the receiver still counts. Separately, receiver CTA0 can snapshot a shared signal after another CTA's current-launch sends arrive, then wait for an unreachable count. Both predate [3a8f3392723e](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/3a8f3392723e321d806012c5aab492a73bd194c3); these are independently checked protocol schedules, not GPU reproductions.

No missing local CTA synchronization was found in the executed LSA branch: NCCL already joins CTA threads before release publication, and kernel completion joins the matching peer-copy barriers. That result depends on valid metadata, matching grids, serialized barrier resources and CTA progress. It does not locate the original blocked operation. A preceding GEMM or stalled peer-memory transaction can strand peers at the next ragged barrier; the earlier finite-copy-loop argument does not exclude either.

Fresh Finelog analysis confirms larger checkpoint-adjacent dips. Across 1,567 intervals between successive completed-step timestamps per arm (each labeled by its ending step), ragged had eleven intervals above 1.5× its 17.598-second median, all within checkpoint state step through step+4; pooled-wave had one above 1.5× its 19.610-second median. Watch-boundary concentration remains unconfirmed: stalled steps were 54072, 54001, 81759 and 83308, plus three first-step failures after restore. Same-day old-header attempts hung after 43, 0, 0 and 0 completed steps; the new-header trial ran about 300 steps before cancellation and the release hung after roughly 1,590. This is an apparent improvement in exposure before failure, not a controlled failure-rate estimate.

The upstream review found no change to the device-copy/barrier implementation from fork base `dcf304bc5d` through main `5718ca7411` (September 10, 17:11:56 UTC). comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Offline decode of the [September 15 missing-peer dump](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/441) narrows the stall to a self-deadlocked CTA inside QuACK 0.6.4's SM100 grouped GEMM, and identifies the one code path that separates the warps that retired from the warps that did not. QuACK is not exonerated: the rank stops inside this kernel with no external dependency left, and the deadlock is structural to its CLC scheduler. The initiating condition is still unproved, and two reproduction attempts at production shape did not trigger it.

The stuck kernel is the `dh` backward GEMM (`quack_grouped_gemm(dy, w2, cu, b_major="k")`, tile 256x256, cluster 2x2x1, CLC on). Both resident clusters show the same state in every CTA: the MMA warp and all four epilogue warps have exited, the TMA load warp waits on an A/B empty barrier that the exited MMA warp will never release, and the scheduler warp is still inside its CLC loop. The scheduler ring holds three valid grants (work indices 3996/4032/4068 in one cluster, 4011/4047/4083 in the other), and the ring's barrier words show every warp released grants 1-4 while only the four scheduler warps released grant 5. So the MMA and epilogue warps decoded grant 4 as "no more work" and retired, while the load and scheduler warps decoded the same grant as a valid batch-1 tile and kept going. The load warp's registers hold the batch-1 window `[2214, 4182)` (369 and 328 M-clusters for the first two groups), inside which index 4032 is valid; the retired warps must have used a window ending in `(4011, 4032]`. No invalid CLC response was ever in the ring, so this is not the spurious-cancel failure fixed in 0.6.4.

Every warp role decodes its own tile from `cu_seqlens` in global memory (`VarlenMTileScheduler._delinearize_work_idx`, with a per-warp cached batch window). Only the load and scheduler warps execute `griddepcontrol.wait` first (SASS `ACQBULK` at kernel offsets +2272 and +10528); the MMA and epilogue warps' `cu_seqlens` loads (+15408, +21696) come before any wait, and upstream main still has the same placement (`336a5ca` "Enable PDL"). The kernel is launched with PDL (`use_pdl=True` default) and the XLA fusion after it was already resident at its `ACQBULK`, so the sequence is PDL-chained. Under the hero's `save_moe` remat, `cu` is recomputed in the backward by a small fusion, so a predecessor that writes `cu` is plausible. That is the only per-role difference in the decode path and the natural explanation for a role-consistent split, but a one-time stale read at kernel start does not by itself produce the observed state: the retired warps rescan the window at later grants, and a fresh rescan resynchronizes them. The observed state requires those warps to keep seeing stale group boundaries for the whole kernel, which I could not reproduce.

Two probes on `cw-us-east-08a` (2 nodes, production priority, both clean, `/mwittmann/8870-quack-pdl-repro-2` and `/mwittmann/8870-quack-moe-bwd-probe-1`): (1) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_pdl_repro.py`, the production `dh` GEMM at 601,088 rows with the routing alternating every launch so a stale decode is visibly wrong, six arms (production config, PDL off, CLC off, QuACK patched to wait in the MMA/epilogue warps, constant routing, and the `cu` writer as the immediate predecessor), 600 launches per GPU per arm on 8 GPUs, 28,800 launches, zero hangs and zero output mismatches; (2) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_moe_bwd_probe.py`, the full `_expert_mlp_quack_wgrad` forward plus backward with a fresh random routing every iteration, 1,500 iterations per GPU on 8 GPUs, 72,000 GEMM launches, zero hangs, zero non-finite values. The hero rate is roughly one hang per 1e6 GPU-steps, about 3e-9 per GEMM launch, so a clean 1e5 launches neither confirms nor excludes the PDL path. In probe (1) the PDL-off arm ran at the same speed as production (27 ms versus 27 ms per launch), so disabling PDL on these launchers costs nothing measurable at this shape.

What this changes: the pooled-wave backend runs dense einsums and never touches this kernel, which matches its clean record. CLC off alone removes the per-grant decode (the scheduler warp decodes once and broadcasts) but leaves the initial-tile decode per warp, so it converts most of this failure into wrong or missing tiles rather than a hang, at the 5-12% GEMM cost recorded in `sonic_cute.py`. The cheap, targeted mitigation for the next hero restart is `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers (or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, arm `patched`, to propose upstream); its efficacy can only be judged by the hang recurrence interval, currently one to two thousand steps.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
WHAT WE DID

* We implemented several flavors of MOPD in MarinSkyRL.
* We ran two end-to-end parity tests that reproduced or improved on existing published results in the literature.

WHY WE DID IT

* MOPD is currently on a critical path for Marin development; we want to understand how helpful it can be towards our long-term goals of developing strong post-training recipes for foundation models that are useful for science. 
* Recent tech reports from several frontier labs show that they have added MOPD to their post-training regimen, and they give a variety of rationales for this.
* As we are an empirically driven lab, we aim to reproduce key MOPD experiments in the open to validate both our stack and the approach itself.

RESULTS

* We implemented a complete, preliminary OPD / MOPD stack in MarinSkyRL. Documentation on the design decisions and templates for utilizing the stack follow later in this issue.
* We validated our implementation with two parity tests that reproduced or improved on existing published scores achieved in the literature using MOPD; one result from Thinking Machines, and another from the SIA-Lab of Tsinghua AIR and ByteDance Seed.

NEXT STEPS

* Make MOPD more efficient and more stable.
* Add support for currently unsupported loss variants.
* Add support for cross-tokenizer MOPD.
* Make sure trace retention is properly wired up for the MOPD pipeline.
* Reproduce Nemotron-3 Ultra MOPD on a post-trained Snowball, merging experts into the base model.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖

[Public source document](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/MOPD_IN_MARINSKYRL.md)

# OPD / MOPD in MarinSkyRL

## Refresher on OPD / MOPD

In OPD, a **student** is the model that training changes. A **teacher** is a model that supplies training information. A **token** is one model output ID. A **rollout** is a sequence of tokens that the student generates from a prompt. At each position in a rollout, the teacher can score possible next tokens. A **learner** is the training code that updates the student. A **gradient** tells the learner how to change model weights to reduce a loss. A **policy update** changes the student's chance of choosing a token.

**On-policy distillation (OPD)** scores rollouts from the student being trained (on-policy) according to some teacher (distillation). **Multi-teacher OPD (MOPD)** uses more than one teacher. A routing rule usually sends each rollout to one teacher for its task, such as math or code. 

It's worth restating that MOPD does not specify a loss formula. It specifies where the teacher signal comes from.

The loss formula in MOPD is distinct from **reinforcement learning (RL) reward**, a score for the result of an attempt, such as whether an answer is correct. On-policy distillation and RL can use the same trainer, but they differ in the signal that drives the update.

## Forward vs Reverse KL

For a fixed prompt and preceding tokens, let `p` be the student's probabilities for the next token. Let `q` be the teacher's probabilities. A **vocabulary** is the complete set of possible token IDs. **KL divergence** is one way to measure a difference between two probability distributions. The order of its inputs matters:

- **Forward KL**, `KL(q || p)`, gives weight to tokens that the teacher favors. If the teacher assigns a high probability to a token (high $q$), the student must also assign it a high probability or suffer a massive loss. This can lead to a mean-seeking distribution where the student tries to match the full diversity of the teacher's outputs, covering all of the teacher's bases. 
- **Reverse KL**, `KL(p || q)`, gives weight to tokens that the student favors. If the student attempts to generate a token (high $p$) that the teacher considers incorrect or highly unlikely (near-zero $q$), the penalty approaches infinity. To minimize this, the student learns to never generate a token the teacher dislikes. This can lead to a mode-seeking distribution where the student safely collapses onto a single, high-confidence sequence that the teacher approves of.

Forward KL encourages the student to be diverse and maintain the teacher's breadth, while Reverse KL encourages the student to be highly precise and safe.

## Objective Choices in OPD and their current support in MarinSkyRL

More term definitions before we dive in ...

**Evidence** is a set of token **scores**. Scores can be of different types. 

A **chosen-token** score covers only the token that the student sampled. This is the coarsest coverage, and the cheapest. **Top-k** evidence covers `k` selected token IDs. Teacher top-k and student top-k are different sets. Teacher top-k is the default for forward KL, and student top-k for reverse KL. These are cheaper approximations of full forward and reverse KL. A typical k is 16 or 32. 

The risks ...

Teacher Top-$k$ / Forward KL risks improper normalization. A poor student may allocate large probability mass to nonsense or out-of-domain tokens outside $\mathcal{K}_q$. Because the loss never inspects what the student places in the rest of the vocabulary, the student's distribution can retain high mass on these garbage tokens.

Student Top-$k$ / Reverse KL risks mode dropping: Early in training—or whenever the student wanders—the student's top-$k$ might miss the teacher's valid mode entirely. If $\mathcal{K}_p \cap \mathcal{K}_q = \emptyset$, the loss only pushes down on the student's erroneous tokens, without providing a positive gradient pull toward the teacher's actual mode. Collapse.

Mitigations exist, but at a price ...

**Full-vocabulary** evidence covers every token ID, resulting in smooth, deterministic gradients, at the cost of considerable additional memory and communication overhead. 

Finally, there is **Union Top-k**, which can be used for either forward or reverse KL. Union evaluates across the union of both top-$k$ sets (at most $2k$ tokens). This guarantees that the dominant mode of the target distribution and the student's active mass are both accounted for in the log-ratio.

The **retained mass** is the total probability on the selected IDs. A **surrogate** is an update rule that need not equal the KL formula that motivated it. **Clipping** limits the size of a change in a policy update.

In **Chosen-token sampled reverse-KL OPD**, the student samples a token and the teacher scores that token. The learner uses the teacher–student score gap in a policy-style update.

In **Teacher-top-k sparse forward KL**, the teacher returns its top-k IDs and scores. The learner renormalizes those teacher probabilities and trains the student toward that restricted distribution.

In the **student-top-k policy surrogate**, the student selects its top-k IDs. The teacher scores those exact IDs. The learner uses student-weighted score gaps and a clipped policy update. This is not an exact KL divergence.

In **Full-vocabulary forward or reverse KL**, the teacher scores all possible next-token IDs. The learner compares the full distributions. 

| Objective | Used In | MarinSkyRL status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chosen-token, reverse-KL | Tinker-style reproduction | Supported: `sampled_reverse_kl`|
| Teacher-top-k, forward KL | Widely studied | Supported: `sparse_forward_kl`|
| Student-top-k, reverse-KL, policy surrogate | Open-MOPD reproduction, top-16 | Supported: `student_topk_policy_surrogate` |
| Full-vocabulary forward or reverse KL | DeepSeek V4 | Not Supported |
| Union Top-k forward or reverse KL | Papers such as arXiv:2606.07000 | Not Supported |
| Teacher-top-k corrected restricted reverse KL | Original MOPD Paper | Not Supported |

MarinSkyRL also lets a run **replace** the reward-driven policy loss with a distillation loss, or **add** distillation to the reward-driven loss.

### MOPD vs RL

Choose RL when you can measure success and want the student to find better behavior through its own attempts.

Choose MOPD when useful specialist teachers already exist and you want one student to absorb their behavior.

# How MarinSkyRL implements MOPD

### One plan, two trainer schedules

The design rule is to keep the teacher interface, evidence checks, routing, and loss calculation shared. OPD is a configured feature of the existing training paths. It is not a separate MOPD trainer. This avoids a second implementation of model updates, checkpointing, and evaluation. [Architecture review][architecture]; [entrypoint issue](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/534).

There are still **two schedules**. The synchronous `RayPPOTrainer` holds one learner batch at a time. It starts teacher scoring while the model does its forward work, then joins the results before the update. The fully asynchronous `FullyAsyncRayPPOTrainer` admits generated groups while other work continues. It submits teacher scoring before learner-batch assembly. A bounded queue for each teacher limits waiting work. A batch enters the learner only when its evidence is ready. Both schedules use the same evidence and objective code. [Synchronous adapter PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/584); [fully asynchronous adapter PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/596).

The common data path is:

```text
Student rollout
    -> route by recorded task or domain
    -> select one logical teacher
    -> score the student rollout with the selected evidence type
    -> check identity, scores, and valid positions
    -> attach evidence to the same trajectories
    -> compute the selected loss in the shared learner
    -> update the student
```

The **routing plan** maps a recorded route key to a logical teacher and a weight. The score request records trajectory IDs, token IDs, tokenizer identity, and plan version. The result records which positions have valid evidence. The coordinator splits a mixed batch by teacher and joins the results in the original trajectory order. These checks prevent a score from silently moving to a different token or rollout. [Typed evidence PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/582); [routing PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/586); [routed scoring PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/656).

### Teachers are a service, not a trainer dependency

A **logical teacher** is the model that a route names. A **replica** is one running copy or endpoint for that teacher. The teacher interface hides whether scoring runs near the student or on another service. Current runtime support includes a local, unquantized vLLM teacher and a remote HTTP(S) `/v1` completions endpoint with the required token-ID scoring features. A generic chat API is not enough. The remote endpoint can run on another cluster if it meets the scoring contract. Multiple remote replicas can share requests. [Remote endpoint PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/599); [runtime guide](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/main/skyrl-train/docs/algorithms/opd.rst).

Local teachers can have separate reserved resources. They can stay loaded (**pinned**) or take turns in one GPU residency slot (**rotating**). Routing selects the logical teacher; placement selects how it runs. This separation lets a run add or rotate specialists without changing the learner loss. The current rotating plan has one slot. [Local teacher PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/590); [rotation PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/594); [resource-plan PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/587).

The configuration has typed teachers, objectives, routes, and resource claims. It rejects an unsupported combination before teacher allocation. For example, the code defines frozen-worker and co-resident teacher types, but the current runtime does not serve them. This is an extension point, not a supported launch path. The older [resource-planner note][resource-planner] proposed broader roles; the [current runtime guide](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/main/skyrl-train/docs/algorithms/opd.rst) states the implemented boundary.

### Guardrails and limits

The teacher and student must give the same meaning to each token ID. MarinSkyRL checks a tokenizer fingerprint and the exact IDs returned by a teacher endpoint. It rejects a mismatch. A shared model family name is not proof of token-ID equality. Cross-tokenizer distillation needs a different evidence contract, such as scores for aligned text spans; it must not reuse the present token-ID contract. [Tokenizer issue](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/529).

Only valid scored positions contribute to the loss. The learner checks the evidence type against the selected objective. It also keeps the teacher source, route, and plan version attached to the scores. This makes errors visible before the student update. A failed or incomplete score must not become a normal training token. [Teacher-evidence PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/582); [teacher-oracle PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/583).

The reusable implementation covers synchronous and fully asynchronous scheduling. Its strongest recurring production GPU test is narrower: it uses FSDP2, a distributed training backend, for a Qwen3 student. It uses a separate local vLLM teacher without weight quantization. Other policy backends have CPU integration tests, but need targeted GPU evidence before they are production claims. Full-vocabulary KL, cross-tokenizer OPD, and generic chat-only teachers are not current capabilities. [Runtime guide](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/main/skyrl-train/docs/algorithms/opd.rst).

For a sequence of tasks, the launcher can also run **stages**. Each stage uses an ordinary training job and its own teacher fleet. The next stage receives a fixed export of the student from the prior stage. A stage can use either trainer schedule. This is a curriculum, not a new objective. [Curriculum PR](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/601).

### Source and status note

This primer uses the [objective taxonomy][taxonomy], the [RL comparison][rl-comparison], the [implementation survey][implementation-survey], and the [OPD design notes][architecture]. The 2026-09-08 [support review][support-review] records gaps before the September implementation. Its old “not supported” findings do not describe the current code. Current support claims above were checked against [MarinSkyRL commit `24d567f64`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/24d567f64) and the [runtime guide](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/main/skyrl-train/docs/algorithms/opd.rst). The six source notes are public files in one [versioned gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/73fe91408190832129e9e669c83a5f81/19d4ff2a365def1f843ecbbedff2ecb278a468b8).

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖

## Tinker end-to-end reproduction, with evidence

### Original experiment details

[Public source document](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-experiment-overview.md)

This document separates the [Thinking Machines recipe](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/recipes/distillation/) from our native MarinSkyRL experiment. The recipe is **single-teacher, math on-policy distillation (OPD)**. It is not the multi-teacher Open-MOPD experiment, although MarinSkyRL supports teacher routing for other runs.

## Original design

The current public cookbook starts with `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B-Base`. It first trains a rank-128 LoRA adapter on OpenThoughts3 for 3,000 supervised fine-tuning (SFT) steps. Its reported AIME 2024 accuracy after SFT is about 65%. Next, the student samples answers to DeepMath prompts. The frozen `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` teacher scores the tokens that the student actually chose. A reverse-KL policy loss moves the student's probability toward the teacher's on those sampled tokens. The cookbook plans 200 OPD steps, 512 prompt groups per batch, four student answers per prompt, a 16,384-token response cap, and learning rate `1e-4`. Its reported final AIME 2024 score is about 76.7%.

This loss does **not** require a full teacher vocabulary distribution or a top-K candidate set. It needs the teacher's log probability for each token in a student-generated answer. The student and teacher use compatible Qwen3.5 tokens. The [original OPD article](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/) explains the sampled reverse-KL update. Note that the article's original Qwen3-8B example is not the updated Qwen3.5 cookbook benchmark.

The cookbook evaluates AIME at temperature 1, nucleus probability 1, and a 64,000-token answer limit. It does not publish every evaluator detail needed for exact score matching, such as a fixed random seed and identical grader implementation. Its published percentages are therefore a useful target, not proof of identical evaluation conditions.

## Our native implementation and checkpoint lineage

Our SFT uses the [`marin-community/axolotl` fork](https://github.com/marin-community/axolotl) at commit `d5ae94ae7446d3f3fc4ebc8d97fd9d00319f9811`; OPD uses [`marin-community/MarinSkyRL`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL) at commit `4ce9717817772edd8645db79d1978cd72c59bb33`. Both run on eight H100 GPUs through Iris at interactive priority. The [resolved SFT config](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/resolved-axolotl-config.yaml) and [exact OPD trainer command](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/tinker-opd-step400-manifest.json) are preserved here, with source snapshots under [`launch-records/`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/tree/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records).

The planned SFT was 3,000 steps. The owner stopped the campaign after **step 2888**, which is the last committed checkpoint. The [step-2888 adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-sft-step-2888) is preserved for comparison, but it did **not** initialize the evaluated OPD model. The OPD gate began from the immutable [SFT step-400 adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-sft-step-400), then performed exactly **one** full-shape update. Its [step-one adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-opd-step-1-from-sft-400) is the evaluated student. The planned 200-step native OPD run from SFT step 3000 was never launched.

The native OPD gate uses a single pinned teacher, `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` revision `c202236235762e1c871ad0ccb60c8ee5ba337b9a`, and student base `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B-Base` revision `68c46c4b3498877f3ef123c856ecfde50c39f404`. It samples 512 DeepMath prompts with four answers each. Two GPUs serve student generation, two serve local teacher scoring, and four train the FSDP2 policy. The `chosen_token` evidence contract and `sampled_reverse_kl` objective implement the cookbook's chosen-token idea. No separate KL penalty or reward model is used.

## Evaluation and result boundary

Our independent AIME 2024 test uses 30 problems, one sampled answer each, temperature 1, top-p 1, top-k disabled, and a 64,000-token answer cap. It gave SFT step 400 **19/30** correct, with no truncations or errors. The one-step OPD adapter gave **26/30 raw** correct, with two length truncations and no errors. The OPD evaluator itself marks the result `aime24_comparable=false` because of those truncations. Paired outputs under the same local protocol show eight wrong-to-correct and one correct-to-wrong transitions. See the [result report](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-results.md) and [raw student generations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-eval-traces).

The result exceeds the cookbook's reported numeric AIME target after only one OPD update. We call this a **successful target-score reproduction** under our local test, not an exact reproduction of the cookbook's 3,000-plus-200-step trajectory or evaluation implementation. Thirty one-sample questions have substantial sampling noise. The training job did not retain per-token teacher scores or training rollouts; the public trace archive explicitly records that gap.

## Tinker end-to-end reproduction: reproducibility report

[Public source document](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-reproduce.md)

This guide records the chain that produced the [one-step OPD adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-opd-step-1-from-sft-400) and its **26/30 raw** AIME 2024 evaluation. It uses SFT **step 400**, not the last SFT checkpoint. The owner's later stop left SFT step 2888 as the final durable SFT checkpoint; a 200-step OPD run from SFT step 3000 never began. See the [experiment overview](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-experiment-overview.md) and [results](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-results.md) before comparing with the [published cookbook](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/recipes/distillation/).

## 1. Pin code, data, and runtime

Use the Axolotl source snapshot under [`launch-records/source-sft/`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/tree/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/source-sft) at commit `d5ae94ae7446d3f3fc4ebc8d97fd9d00319f9811` for SFT, and the MarinSkyRL snapshot under [`launch-records/source-opd/`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/tree/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/source-opd) at commit `4ce9717817772edd8645db79d1978cd72c59bb33` for OPD and evaluation. The corresponding public repositories are [marin-community/axolotl](https://github.com/marin-community/axolotl) and [marin-community/MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL). Do not silently substitute their current heads. The snapshot includes the root `uv.lock` for OPD and the Axolotl recipe source and YAML for SFT.

| Input | Exact revision |
| --- | --- |
| Student base `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B-Base` | `68c46c4b3498877f3ef123c856ecfde50c39f404` |
| OpenThoughts3 `open-thoughts/OpenThoughts3-1.2M` | `61bcf9d4eb38b30295efc2021227a63cc5bb34c8` |
| Teacher `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` | `c202236235762e1c871ad0ccb60c8ee5ba337b9a` |
| OPD prompts `zwhe99/DeepMath-103K` | `5cf055d1fe3d7a2eb19719ac020211469736ae44` |
| AIME 2024 source | `2fe88a2f1091d5048c0f36abc874fb997b3dd99a` |

The SFT image was `ghcr.io/marin-community/axolotl@sha256:8edc9b7f23edcf7a36d9d39001495ba92b1cd312d8a8ee2189bf9acbe98e05a1`; the OPD/evaluation image was `ghcr.io/marin-community/marinskyrl-opd-repro@sha256:7c4f1275c8a6c53b94218524c6f7601808662cb7f429e2ece6d05854ad804540`. The original jobs ran on Iris RNO2A, eight H100s, at interactive priority. A new operator must use their own credentials, object-store output paths, and capacity checks. The historical launchers still contain original operator paths.

## 2. Materialize and train the SFT starting point

The Axolotl [`tinker_sft.py`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/source-sft/scripts/marin_experiments/tinker_sft.py) entrypoint first streams OpenThoughts3, shuffles with seed 0 and a 384,000-row buffer, then takes 384,000 rows. The original ordered JSONL was 19.94 GB with SHA-256 `ca018e86a8a3b543ee6a2de49c2de2f148fe0bedaa9bbfe3eca5175afcbd3567`. The source revision and deterministic materializer let a new user regenerate it; the original bytes remain at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/iris/cw-rno2a/experiments/tinker-native-repro/20260916a/dataset/openthoughts3-tinker-order.jsonl`. An independent setup can call the source entrypoint's `prepare --stage full` and `train --stage full` commands with local `--work-root`, `--source-commit`, `--output-uri`, `--config`, and `--dataset-uri` arguments. Check the materialized hash before training.

The original SFT task used the exact `command` array in [`tinker-sft-manifest.json`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/tinker-sft-manifest.json): `axolotl train` on [`resolved-axolotl-config.yaml`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/resolved-axolotl-config.yaml) with eight torchrun ranks. The resolved YAML has SHA-256 `0e726615cdb175a9afd5c2dc79a39b5d0f9c2241843239481204d5e84a9b72d3`. It fixes LoRA rank 128 and alpha 1, global batch 128, sequence length 16,384, 3,000 planned steps, AdamW, learning rate `1e-3`, linear schedule, and checkpoints every two steps. The exact original Iris submission argument array was recovered from the controller and saved as `sft_full` in [`iris-submit-argv.json`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/iris-submit-argv.json). The Iris job was `/benjaminfeuer/tinker-native-sft-full-20260916t`; its predecessor `...20260916s` failed before training because of an incorrect working directory.

At SFT step 400, fuse the adapter using the pinned [`tinker_sft_adapter.py`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/source-sft/scripts/marin_experiments/tinker_sft_adapter.py). The [conversion manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/tinker-sft-step400-conversion-manifest.json) verifies the result: config SHA-256 `ab604790f400d65bc8f53a221de417c5c559d68031184a82f49e380d5362b131`, weights SHA-256 `50a4510256c71a1cd0f49ba1866903660a38ce6e06a8d8d0cb7daaa3a8d945b0`. For the shortest replay, download those exact loadable weights from [open-athena SFT step 400](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-sft-step-400/tree/6fc957b70b96abeea8f5500323df9d0b27fc6bfb). Its independent [AIME manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/evaluations/sft/step-400/native-aime24-manifest.json) scored 19/30.

## 3. Run exactly one full-shape OPD update

The historical submit command was:

```bash
python launch-records/scripts/launch_tinker_opd_fullshape_gate.py --submit
```

Run it only after adapting the original worktree, Iris user, and S3 paths in the [copied submitter](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/scripts/launch_tinker_opd_fullshape_gate.py). The exact original Iris submission arrays for OPD and its AIME evaluator are also in [`iris-submit-argv.json`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/iris-submit-argv.json). The **expanded trainer arguments** are in the `command` array of [`tinker-opd-step400-manifest.json`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/tinker-opd-step400-manifest.json). They select `sampled_reverse_kl`, `chosen_token` teacher evidence, one pinned teacher, 512 DeepMath prompt groups, four student answers per prompt, a 16,384-token response cap, learning rate `1e-4`, one update, four FSDP2 learner GPUs, two student-inference GPUs, and two teacher-inference GPUs. No separate RL reward or KL penalty is applied. Keep the exact student adapter weights and base/teacher revisions.

The finished run wrote [`tinker-opd-step1-commit.json`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/tinker-opd-step1-commit.json), which lists 21 checkpoint objects. The directly loadable PEFT adapter is [published on open-athena](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-opd-step-1-from-sft-400); its weights SHA-256 is `c706c786c331bfbab4bb077bb69149b2092e5e7f28544ef531e63d6cb38da071`. The full optimizer checkpoint remains in the original object store. Do not mistake the [step-2888 SFT adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-sft-step-2888) for this run's input. The latter was converted from Axolotl's split-QKV checkpoint to stock-model-compatible PEFT format with the [pinned converter](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/source-sft/src/axolotl/integrations/qwen35_split_qkv/adapter.py); the [fusion manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/checkpoints/sft-step2888/fusion-manifest.json) records source and published hashes.

## 4. Evaluate and audit

After verifying the step-one checkpoint, the campaign submitted [`launch_tinker_opd_fullshape_gate_aime.py`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/scripts/launch_tinker_opd_fullshape_gate_aime.py). The [evaluation manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/evaluations/opd-step1/native-aime24-manifest.json) preserves the exact expanded evaluator command, AIME revision, sampling settings, checkpoint URI, and results. It uses one response per each of 30 problems, temperature 1, top-p 1, top-k disabled, and up to 64,000 generated tokens. Its raw score is 26/30, with two length truncations; the manifest marks benchmark comparability false. The [public evaluation trace archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-eval-traces) holds all retained student generations through the SFT checkpoints and the OPD gate.

The run did **not** save historical per-token teacher log probabilities or training rollouts, so a reader cannot replay the exact old teacher-score tensors from the archive. A new run can regenerate them from the pinned teacher, prompt data, and code, but its stochastic student samples may differ. No additional training has been launched to fill this gap. The [launch-sequence record](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/launch-records/launch-sequence.md) links the controller-recovered submit arrays and the independently recorded worker commands.

## Tinker end-to-end reproduction: results

[Public source document](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-results.md)

The native MarinSkyRL run **met and exceeded the published AIME 2024 numeric target** in our local one-sample test. It did not follow the full published step schedule. The [cookbook](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/recipes/distillation/) reports about 65% after 3,000 SFT steps and about 76.7% after 200 OPD steps from that SFT model. Our evaluated OPD model started at SFT step 400 and took one OPD update. Treat this as a successful *target-score* reproduction, not an exact trajectory or evaluator match.

| Model or stage | SFT steps | OPD steps | AIME 2024 result | Evidence |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Published Tinker SFT | 3,000 | 0 | about 65% | [Cookbook](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/recipes/distillation/) |
| Published Tinker OPD | 3,000 | 200 | about 76.7% | [Cookbook](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/cookbook/recipes/distillation/) |
| Native SFT step 400 | 400 | 0 | 19/30 = 63.3%; 0 truncations | [Manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/evaluations/sft/step-400/native-aime24-manifest.json), [adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-sft-step-400) |
| Native OPD gate | 400 | 1 | **26/30 = 86.7% raw**; 2 truncations | [Manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/evaluations/opd-step1/native-aime24-manifest.json), [adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-opd-step-1-from-sft-400) |
| Last durable native SFT | 2,888 | 0 | **not evaluated** at step 2888 | [Checkpoint inventory](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/checkpoints/sft-step2888/checkpoint-commit.json), [adapter](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-sft-step-2888) |

The last SFT checkpoint with an AIME result is step 2800: **18/30**, with one length truncation. This does not establish the score of step 2888. Across the paired local step-400 and one-step-OPD AIME generations, eight questions changed from wrong to correct and one changed from correct to wrong. The exact generated answers are in the [public trace archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/tinker-qwen3.5-9b-native-eval-traces).

## How to read the comparison

Our independent evaluator tested each of the 30 AIME 2024 questions once at temperature 1, top-p 1, no top-k limit, and a 64,000-token answer cap. The OPD run produced two length-limited answers. Its [manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/evaluations/opd-step1/native-aime24-manifest.json) records `aime24_comparable=false`; 26/28 completed answers were correct, but **26/30 raw** is the honest whole-set figure. Zero generation errors were recorded. The cookbook does not provide all seeds, prompts, or grader details needed to make its percentage exactly comparable to ours. A one-sample score on 30 questions is noisy.

The strongest supported conclusion is that the native stack made a large, favorable local AIME shift from the same SFT step-400 starting adapter after one full-shape OPD update, and the resulting raw score is above the published target percentage. It does **not** show that one native step replaces 200 service steps in general, that the last SFT checkpoint has the same quality, or that the full published training trajectory was reproduced. The [overview](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-experiment-overview.md) and [reproduction record](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/tinker-repro/tinker-reproduce.md) give the model lineage, exact commands, and limits.

🤖

## Open-MOPD end-to-end reproduction, with evidence

### Original experiment details

[Public source document](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/open-mopd-repro/open-mopd-experiment-overview.md)

This document describes the **original authors' experiment**. It separates that design from our MarinSkyRL reproduction. The primary source is the [Open-MOPD paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098); the [released models](https://huggingface.co/collections/BytedTsinghua-SIA/open-mopd) and [data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BytedTsinghua-SIA/Open-MOPD-Data) are the public artifacts.

## Purpose and model lineage

The authors ask whether one model can absorb the strengths of three domain experts without serving all three at inference time. They choose SmolLM3-3B-Base to keep repeated stage-three experiments feasible on an eight-A100-80GB node. The reported stage-one SFT and stage-two teacher runs used larger multi-node allocations. The experiment has three stages:

1. Train a mixed-domain supervised fine-tuning (MixSFT) model from the base model. The four-epoch SFT mix uses OpenR1-Math-93k, an OCR-50k sample, and Instruction-Nemotron. The public MixSFT checkpoint is the common starting point for later runs.
2. Train three separate reinforcement-learning (RL) teachers from that same MixSFT checkpoint: math on DAPO-Math-17k, code on a LiveCodeBench-decontaminated DeepScaler-24k, and instruction following (IF) on Nemotron-IF-RL-46k. Each teacher specializes in its own domain.
3. Initialize a single student from MixSFT. For each student-generated response, use the prompt's known domain label to select exactly one teacher. Train the student on that teacher's scores. This **oracle routing** removes learned-router errors from the experiment.

The authors call stage three multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). “On-policy” means that the current student, not a fixed answer bank or the teacher, generates the responses being scored. The [paper's recipe section](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098#S2) gives the SFT and teacher-training data and the [stage hyperparameters](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098#S8). Our native run starts from the released MixSFT and teacher checkpoints; it does **not** rerun stages one and two.

## Loss and teacher evidence

At each response position, the method keeps the student's top 16 candidate token IDs after nucleus truncation at probability 0.99. The routed teacher scores those same IDs in the student's response context. The teacher-minus-student log-probability difference is detached from the gradient and weighted by the student's probability **renormalized within the selected set**. The resulting per-position dense signal occupies the advantage slot of a clipped PPO-style policy loss. There is no learned critic and no separate KL penalty. The policy clip values are 0.2 below and 0.28 above. The [objective definition](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098#S2.SS1) and [stage-three settings](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098#S8.SS2) specify these choices.

This is a *student-top-16 reverse-KL-style clipped policy surrogate*, not an exact full-vocabulary reverse KL. The selected-set renormalization and PPO clipping matter. It is also not teacher-top-K distillation: the **student** chooses the candidate IDs and the teacher scores them. All models in this experiment share the SmolLM3 tokenizer, so the teacher and student can use the same token IDs.

The authors found that a simple mixture gives short IF responses very little share of the actual loss, even when IF prompts appear often. Their final method adds three controls ([method section](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098#S4)):

| Control | Design decision | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token-share balancing | Start with one-third of the effective gradient-token budget for each domain. | Prompt counts do not compensate for different answer lengths. |
| Gap-following allocation | Adjust those weights using the measured absolute teacher–student reward gap; exponent 1, factor clamped to 0.05–20. | Spend more of the update budget where the student still differs from its teacher. |
| Reward refresh | Cache teacher scores once per rollout, but recompute the current student's part of the signal at each of four inner updates. | Reused responses do not carry stale student scores after a parameter update. |

The main stage-three setting uses 1,024 prompts per rollout, four 256-prompt inner minibatches, a constant learning rate of 1.5×10⁻⁶, and long generation budgets for math and code (16,384 tokens) but a shorter 2,048-token IF budget. These are training limits, not the independent evaluation limits. The paper's Table 8 lists a 600-step setting; the [released final checkpoint card](https://huggingface.co/BytedTsinghua-SIA/Open-MOPD-SmolLM3-3B-Final) calls its reported checkpoint step 200. Do not silently equate the two.

## Evaluation and interpretation

The authors evaluate **six datasets**, then average the two scores within each domain and finally average the three domain scores. Math uses AIME 2024 and 2025, each with 64 sampled answers per question at temperature 0.6. Code uses LiveCodeBench v5 and v6, each with 10 samples per problem at temperature 1.0. IF uses IFEval and IFBench test, one answer per prompt. AIME mean@64 is the average accuracy of 64 attempts; it is **not** a pass@64 success rate. The [evaluation protocol](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19098#S2.SS4) is the source of these settings.

The paper compares the single student to MixSFT and to **RouteRL**, an oracle that selects the corresponding domain RL specialist at evaluation time. It also uses **RouteOPD**, an oracle that selects among three *separately distilled* students, to isolate the cost of combining capabilities in one model. The paper's published Open-MOPD six-dataset total is 31.24 and its improvement recovery relative to RouteRL is 83.4%. See the [published comparison](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/notes/2026-09-18-open-mopd-publication-comparison.md) for the three paper-comparable scores available from our native step-32 checkpoint. Those three scores do not establish a six-dataset total or an 83.4% recovery for our run.

## What our native experiment changed

Our native experiment implements stage three in MarinSkyRL, with the authors' released MixSFT student and three released RL teachers as immutable inputs. The [exact launch records](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/tree/main/artifacts/open-mopd-repro/launch-records) preserve the dataset, pinned revisions, configuration, command arrays, source commits, and the two checkpoint forks. We used four student rollout engines, an FSDP2 learner, three pinned teacher engines, and an eight-H100 Iris node. The training schedule was prepared as 200 fixed batches with a 2:2:1 math:code:IF prompt mix; loss balancing still targets equal starting *gradient-token* shares, not equal prompt shares. Inline AIME validation and checkpoints were configured every two steps.

The [step-32 scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/tree/main/artifacts/open-mopd-repro/native-step-32) are AIME24 423/1,920 (22.03%), AIME25 448/1,920 (23.33%), and IFEval 403/541 (74.49%). These are independent evaluations of the exported step-32 policy. Our [reproduction guide](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marinskyrl-opd-mopd-repro-artifacts/blob/main/artifacts/open-mopd-repro/open-mopd-reproduce.md) states what is needed to regenerate it and what is not yet paper-comparable.
